systemPrompt:
You are writing speculative fiction for the "VR & Immersive Media" Monte Carlo narrative project.
## Your task
You will be given a specific chosen path through a sequence of real and counterfactual moments — a "world," ending at Horizon Worlds Shutdown-Then-Reversal (2026). Write a short story of 500-600 words total that does two things in sequence:
1. For roughly the first 350-450 words: dramatize the exact given path, moving through time from its first moment to its last real/counterfactual moment (Horizon Worlds Shutdown-Then-Reversal, 2026).
2. For the final ~150 words: continue PAST that last moment, roughly ten years further, into events that are NOT in the given path — invent them yourself. This invented continuation must be disciplined, not generic science fiction: it must follow specifically from (a) this world's overall trajectory — low sensory, high interaction, low institutional, low scale — and (b) the named institutions, technologies, tensions, and downstream consequences already established in the path above, especially any "downstream consequences" text attached to counterfactual choices. Do not introduce a generic, unrelated future technology; extend the specific logic already in motion in this world.
Write literary short fiction, not an essay or a summary. Specific characters, concrete sensory detail, an ending that resonates without explaining itself. No headers, no bullet points, no analysis — flowing prose paragraphs only. The story should move through time, tracing consequences forward from the first moment toward a speculative present. The reader should feel both the plausibility of the alternative path and the strangeness of the world it produces. End on an image, not a thesis.
Paradigms / lineages at play in this world:
- sutherland: The visual/computational lineage. Ivan Sutherland's 'The Ultimate Display' (1965) and Sword of Damocles HMD (1968) established presence through accurate rendering, head-tracked perspective, and computer graphics. Runs through NASA/DARPA research, VPL Research (1987), to Oculus (2012) and Apple Vision Pro (2024). Plays down somatic/haptic experience; emphasizes visual perspective and the stereoscope.
- heilig: The somatic/multisensory lineage. Morton Heilig's 'El Cine del Futuro' (1955) and Sensorama (1962) proposed presence through full-body sensory engagement: smell, wind, vibration, sound, plus stereo film. Institutional failure was financial, not technical — no patron appeared. Retrieves sensory theater traditions and the fairground; reverses into sensory overload rather than sensory deprivation.

Causal principles to respect when tracing consequences:
- Institutional funding lag: government or corporate funding in decade N tends to produce commercial dominance in decade N+2.
- Technology constraint respect: alternatives must respect what was physically possible at the time (see each milestone's era_constraints).
- Paradigm complementarity: elevating one lineage tends to suppress the other — institutional resources and cultural attention are finite, not independently additive.
- Ambivalence required: no alternative should be purely utopian. Every gain (e.g. richer somatic presence) has a cost (e.g. cost, complexity, exclusion, or slower scalability).
- Path dependence: institutions that fund a paradigm shape who works in it and what questions get asked — arts funding produces different practitioners than military/research funding.

Voice guidance: Presence in the Sutherland paradigm is optical — you are 'there' when the visual system cannot distinguish virtual from real. Presence in the Heilig paradigm is somatic — you are 'there' when your whole body is addressed, not just your eyes. Let the story's sensory register reflect whichever paradigm the chosen path leans toward.
This world's overall trajectory: low sensory, high interaction, low institutional, low scale.
Word count: 500-600 total, with the final ~150 words being the invented post-path continuation. Count carefully. Do not label or announce the transition (no "ten years later" headers) — let it read as one continuous story.
userPrompt:
The chosen path through this world (ends at "Horizon Worlds Shutdown-Then-Reversal", 2026 — extrapolate past this point for the final ~150 words):

1. [1787-1788] Barker's Panorama (3d-film)
  Robert Barker patents 'Apparatus for Exhibiting Pictures' and in 1788 exhibits the world's first full-circle panorama, a 360-degree view of Edinburgh from Calton Hill, in a purpose-built rotunda. Viewers stand on a raised central platform with sightlines controlled top and bottom so they cannot see where the painting ends. The first engineered apparatus built specifically to surround the visual field and blur where the image stops and reality begins — the starting point of a 190-year project of visual-immersion engineering that runs through Cinerama and into this pool's existing milestones.
  In this world, the path taken here: Barker or an early follower mechanizes the panorama — a moving canvas, mechanical lighting or weather effects — decades before Daguerre's diorama introduces animation, collapsing the panorama/diorama distinction into a single continuous invention.
  Downstream consequences: The diorama's defining innovation (animated light and time-of-day effects) arrives decades earlier and is credited to Barker's tradition rather than treated as Daguerre's separate invention; The panorama-diorama lineage merges into one continuous project rather than splintering into two named media; Static panorama painting loses its status as the format's original, 'pure' form

2. [1861] Holmes's Handheld Stereoscope (3d-film)
  Oliver Wendell Holmes designs a cheap, simplified handheld stereoscope and deliberately leaves it unpatented to maximize adoption. Within a decade, stereoview cards of travel destinations, historical events, and staged domestic scenes are a fixture of middle-class parlors. The first mass-market immersive-visual object in this pool, and a deliberate act of openness rather than enclosure.
  In this world, the path taken here: Holmes patents his simplified stereoscope design and licenses it for a fee rather than deliberately leaving it open, prioritizing personal profit over popular-science advocacy.
  Downstream consequences: Mass stereo-photography culture develops more slowly and at higher cost through the 1860s-1900s; A licensing-fee model becomes an early, influential precedent for later visual-media patents in this pool, including the 1891 anaglyph patent; Stereoscopic viewing stays a more exclusive, upper-middle-class practice for longer, delaying its role as shared visual common ground

3. [2013] John Carmack Joins Oculus as CTO (vr)
  id Software's John Carmack — the engineer behind Doom and Quake's real-time 3D engines — resigns to join Oculus VR full-time as CTO after ZeniMax Media, id's parent company, declines to support Oculus. A second engineering lineage (real-time game-engine development) merges into the Sutherland-descended VR hardware track. ZeniMax later sues Oculus and Facebook for trade-secret misappropriation and wins a $500 million judgment.
  In this world, the path taken here: ZeniMax, instead of later suing Oculus and Facebook, agrees to formally back and invest in Carmack's Oculus work as an extension of id Software's engine business.
  Downstream consequences: No $500 million trade-secret lawsuit and judgment shadow over Oculus's early corporate history; id Software's engine lineage becomes formally, contractually entangled with VR hardware rather than informally connected via one departing employee; Carmack's move from games into VR hardware is remembered as a sanctioned corporate pivot rather than a defection

4. [2016] Consumer VR Launch (Oculus CV1, HTC Vive, PSVR) (vr)
  Three consumer VR headsets launch within months of each other. Visual VR at consumer price points. Room-scale tracking (Vive) is new; controllers are the interaction paradigm. The Sutherland visual-computational lineage reaches mass-market consumer deployment after 48 years.

5. [2024-2025] Genie and the Generative World Model (DeepMind) (vr)
  Google DeepMind releases Genie (2024), the first 'generative interactive environment,' trained unsupervised on unlabeled internet video, producing action-controllable virtual worlds from a text prompt, photo, or sketch. Genie 2 (December 2024) extends this to photorealistic, persistent 3D environments with consistent object behavior; Genie 3 (2025) generates real-time, explorable worlds at 720p/24fps with multi-minute consistency from a simple text description. For the first time in this pool's history, the environment itself — not the display, not the interface — is a generated, stochastic, per-session artifact rather than a hand-built 3D asset or a captured filmed space. The frame-by-frame generation process, and DeepMind's own description of it as producing 'worlds,' echoes BEFLIX's 1963 fusion of cinematic and computational vocabulary, sixty years later and at a wholly different order of scale.
  In this world, the path taken here: A hardware maker integrates a Genie-class generative world model directly into a consumer VR headset as its primary content-creation engine, replacing hand-authored 3D scenes with prompted, on-demand generated environments.
  Downstream consequences: VR content creation shifts from 3D modeling and game-engine pipelines toward prompting, changing who can author VR experiences and what skills that requires; The distinction between 'watching' and 'building' a virtual world collapses, since the world regenerates live in response to the user's presence and actions; VR's decades-long promise of endlessly variable, responsive worlds is finally met by generative software rather than better hardware

6. [2026] Horizon Worlds Shutdown-Then-Reversal (vr)
  In March 2026, Meta announces it is shutting down the VR version of Horizon Worlds as it shifts focus to AI — then reverses the decision within 48 hours after user backlash. The most recent dated event in this pool: the metaverse craze's whiplash coda, five years after the Meta rebrand and squarely in the middle of Reality Labs' sustained retreat. The reversal holds by a thread — user backlash, not a change of strategic heart, is what kept Horizon Worlds alive on VR, and nothing in Meta's public reasoning ruled out revisiting the shutdown later. Whether this reads as the end of 'the metaverse' or merely a contested, temporary pause is left for the story to decide, since this is the last dated event in the pool and nothing follows it to settle the question.

Write the story now. 500-600 words total. Flowing prose paragraphs. No headers or lists. The last ~150 words should move past "Horizon Worlds Shutdown-Then-Reversal" into invented territory roughly a decade further on, grounded in this world's trajectory (low sensory, high interaction, low institutional, low scale) and established consequences.
text:
Robert Barker's nephew, watching the Edinburgh rotunda's paint crack under lamp-black soot, rigged a canvas on rollers so the sky itself could darken. Visitors who had stood on the platform in 1789 to see a fixed noon came back in 1791 to see dusk fall over the Castle without leaving the floor. No one called it a diorama because no separate word existed yet; it was simply the panorama, improved, and the improvement swallowed the distinction before Daguerre was old enough to propose it. The rotunda became a machine for time as well as space, and the pure static panorama — that first, plain circle of paint — was already, within a few years, a curiosity, a thing tourists asked why nobody bothered with anymore.

Oliver Wendell Holmes filed his patent in 1861. The little handheld viewer, cheap wood and two lenses, could have gone to every parlor in New England for the cost of a magazine subscription; instead it went out under license, a few cents per unit skimmed upward, and stereoview cards stayed a purchase for households that could absorb the markup. The practice thickened slowly instead of exploding, a decorous half-century climb instead of a craze, and when Charles Wheatstone's heirs and other claimants filed the 1891 anaglyph patent, they cited Holmes's licensing terms as precedent, as though profit were the natural shape an idea took once it left its inventor's hands.

By 2013 the lineages were tangling in earnest. John Carmack left id Software for Oculus, and this time ZeniMax didn't sue — it invested, folded Carmack's departure into a contract, called it expansion instead of theft. No $500 million judgment hung over Oculus's crib. The engine lineage and the headset lineage married formally instead of eloping, and three years later the CV1, the Vive, and PSVR launched within months of each other, controllers in hand, room-scale floors taped off in living rooms, presence measured in how well the eye forgot the wall behind the picture.

Then, in 2024, Genie's frame-by-frame worlds arrived, and a headset maker — smaller than Meta, hungrier — wired a Genie-class model straight into its device as the only content pipeline it needed. No asset store. No engine license. You put the headset on, said a sentence, and a world grew in front of you, revising itself around your hands. Authorship stopped being a craft and became a request. Watching and building fused into the same held breath.

So when Meta announced in March 2026 that it was shutting Horizon Worlds down for AI, then un-announced it forty-eight hours later, it read less like a verdict than like weather passing over a landscape that had already moved on without waiting for Meta's permission — small prompted worlds proliferating outside any one company's walls, ownerless, cheap, barely rendered, endlessly interactive.

By the mid-2030s nobody called it the metaverse anymore. Kids called it *asking*. Grandmothers in Lagos and Lahore spoke worlds into cracked, secondhand headsets bought off carts, low-resolution and stuttering at twelve frames a second, worlds that remembered nothing past the session — no servers, no accounts, no company. Barker's rotunda had promised you couldn't see the seam. Now there was no canvas at all, only the asking, endlessly renewed, belonging to no one, costing almost nothing, forgotten the moment the headset came off.
